hints: Look carefully at where each label is pointing, starting from the airway lumen at the top and moving outwards. Which layer looks like the tall, ciliated lining and which looks deeper and more fibrous?
Remember which tissue type in the trachea and bronchioles is contractile. Think about smooth muscle versus supporting cartilage, lining epithelium and loose connective tissue.
walkthrough:
**Orientate yourself in the section**

Start at the white space at the top. That is the lumen of the trachea. Moving downwards you pass through the wall layers in order: lining epithelium, underlying connective tissue, glands and muscle, then cartilage on the outside.

**Identify what each label shows**

Label A points to the tall lining with cilia and goblet cells. That is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium. Label B points to the loose tissue just beneath it. That is connective tissue of the lamina propria. Deeper down, label D points to a band of spindle shaped fibres. That appearance is typical of smooth muscle. Label C points to the paler, more uniform tissue at the bottom right. That is cartilage.

**Link structure to contraction**

Only muscle tissue can actively contract and relax to change airway diameter. Epithelium moves mucus, connective tissue supports, and cartilage holds the trachea open but cannot contract. Therefore the smooth muscle band at D is the answer.

options.A: This is the ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. It traps and sweeps mucus, but it cannot contract to change diameter.
options.B: This is loose connective tissue beneath the epithelium. It supports and supplies the lining, but it is not contractile.
options.C: This is cartilage. It provides rigid C-shaped support to prevent collapse, but it cannot contract and relax.
options.D: This is the layer of smooth muscle. It contracts to narrow and relaxes to widen the airways, controlling airflow and diameter.
